title: Anomalous First Passage in Evolution: Edge-KPZ Theory
abstract: The pace of evolution depends on how rapidly new phenotypes arise. We show that neutral Wright-Fisher evolution exhibits anomalous first passage despite diffusive mutations. The mean time for the first individual to reach a prescribed phenotypic distance scales approximately as $(σ^2)^{-3/2}$ with mutation variance $σ^2$. Two crossovers bound this regime, with inverse-variance scaling on either side. Combining coalescent theory with Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) fluctuations at the dilute population edge, we develop an edge-KPZ theory of all three regimes. The anomaly persists under weak selection.
summary: This theoretical paper develops an edge-KPZ theory to explain the anomalous scaling of the first passage time in neutral population evolution. By combining coalescent theory with the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation, the authors show that the time to reach a distant phenotype scales anomalously with mutation variance. This work provides a deep link between population genetics and non-equilibrium statistical physics.
main_problem: The paper investigates the anomalous scaling of the first passage time (FPT) in evolutionary dynamics, specifically how the time required for a phenotype to reach a distant state is determined by mutation and population fluctuations.
main_result: Neutral Wright-Fisher evolution exhibits an anomalous FPT scaling proportional to $	ilde{L}^3$ in an intermediate regime, which is described by an edge-KPZ theory.
method: The authors combine coalescent theory with the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation, analyzing the evolution of the population density via stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) and using Cole-Hopf transformations.
model_or_system: The model is neutral Wright-Fisher evolution, where phenotypic change is driven by Gaussian mutations ($\sigma^2$) and population dynamics are governed by density evolution equations. The analysis focuses on the separation distribution of two lineages over time.
key_observables: Mean first-passage time ($\langle T_L angle$), population density $ho(x, t)$, and the separation probability $p_{	ext{pair}}(S)$.
important_parameters: Mutation variance ($\sigma^2$), population size ($N$), and the target phenotypic distance ($L$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the diffusion approximation for smooth densities and uses scaling limits ($	ilde{t} = t/N$) to derive continuum equations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the anomalous scaling of $\langle T_L angle$ vs. $\sigma^2$ (showing $\propto (\sigma^2)^{-3/2}$) and confirm the scaling collapse of FPT data onto a master curve.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical problem (FPT in evolution) to deriving the continuum SPDE for density evolution, linking this to coalescence theory, and finally applying the KPZ framework to establish the three distinct scaling regimes ($	ilde{L}^2 	o 	ilde{L}^3 	o 	ilde{L}^2$).
why_interesting: The connection between population genetics (Wright-Fisher model) and non-equilibrium statistical physics tools like KPZ theory provides a powerful, universal framework for understanding how collective fluctuations dictate macroscopic evolutionary rates.
